verdicts.why: Both sheets spell the name exactly, add nothing, and use the same bold grotesque wordmark, so the marks decide it. B is a solid heartwood disc with a wedge cut into it, like a felling notch in a log. It holds as a clean, distinct shape at 16 and 32 px, and its few thick areas would cut cleanly in vinyl and embroider well. A's nested rings with a center dot and thin white gaps turn into a muddy bullseye at 16 px, and it reads more like a generic target than a tree.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing; both use the same idea, a cut growth-ring cross-section set in the same grotesque type. A uses two heavy rings, so it stays a clean, recognizable shape at 16 and 32 px and has no thin gaps to lose in embroidery or cut vinyl. B's three rings, small center dot and thin white gaps fill in at 16 px, and the mark also reads as a generic bullseye or target.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing, and both marks keep their shape at 16 and 32 px and in one color and reversed. B's split disc is the cleaner, more deliberate form, with solid weights that will stamp and embroider well. A's blocky pixel 'B' looks like a crude 8-bit initial with uneven, arbitrary counters and no tie to the mill, the falls or roasting. B's idea is still weak: it reads as a flattened coffee bean or a generic horizon disc, close to the cliché the brief ruled out, so its lead is mostly on craft.

Both spell the name exactly, add nothing, and hold up at 16 px, in one color and reversed. A's mark is a solid dark disc cut by a thick horizontal band. It reads as dark water at a horizon, its heavy shapes would stamp and embroider cleanly, and it pairs well with the refined serif. B's chunky, pixel-style stepped 'B' also survives at small sizes, but it looks like an 8-bit glyph with uneven counters. That has nothing to do with a 1940s feed mill and clashes with the serif wordmark. A's split circle is close to generic and could be read as a coffee bean's crease, so its lead is small.

The two pages share nearly the same layout and system, so small errors decide it. B has visible slips: the footer lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg', 'For Locals' is wrongly capitalized, a '2026' date was added, and it names Fraunces as the logo face even though its logo samples are set in a different serif. A's Bitter/Source Sans pairing matches its logo, and its intro names Erik and Nils. B's color names (Bank Vault Cream, Kettle Steam) and its imagery rule showing the brothers fit the client a little better, but that doesn't make up for its sloppier page.

The two pages share the same layout and structure, so small craft and accuracy points decide it. A has visible errors: the footer lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg', 'Locals' is wrongly capitalized, and it names Fraunces for the logo when the logo shown is a different slab serif. B pairs Bitter, which matches the wordmark, with Source Sans 3, names the Lund brothers from the brief, and gives more specific imagery rules (the brewhouse shot in daylight, cans on a county shelf, and no faces or dogs without a yes).

council: '2026' date on the guide, which the brief does not give

verdicts.why: A shows the logo on three backgrounds with clear-space and minimum-size rules, labels its imagery rules as Do and Don't, and gives two Say/Not pairs built from facts in the brief. B leaves its two picture columns unlabeled, so a reader has to guess which list is allowed. B also says photos should be 'close enough to see the tool,' which works against the nervous adults the practice serves, while A specifically rules out frightening close-ups of drills and needles. B has a large empty gap under its type section and its picture list runs into the footer; A has small slips of its own, such as the white-on-teal tile labelled 14.1:1 when it should be about 9.5:1, but it is the more complete and usable system.

Neither page invents facts, and both use nearly the same palette and type scale. B does more of the job a system needs to do: it shows the logo on light, dark and teal grounds with clear-space and minimum-size rules, lists contrast pairs with what each one passes, and gives two Say/Not voice pairs written for nervous adults returning after years away. A is clean but thin: its logo guidance is one footnote, its type block leaves an empty gap, and it has only one voice example. B's imagery rules are also easier to judge a photo against (eye level, no frightening drill close-ups, consent for before-and-after shots), though its small teal logo tile and some minor mismatches between swatch and table contrast ratios are small craft flaws.

nocouncil: '2026' date label on the guide is not from the brief (minor)

verdicts.why: Both use the brief's facts correctly. B looks more like a finished product: the intermediate stops are unlabeled dots instead of A's placeholder-looking 'Stop / Stop' rows, the primary action sits at the bottom within thumb reach, and offline mode greys the bus marker and says 'Last known position', so the stale data shows at a glance. A's offline explanation is wordier but very clear, which keeps the margin slight.

Both use only the brief's facts: Maya, bus 14, morning route, Oak St. and Ridgeway Ave., 3 stops, about 6 minutes, Mr. Dorsey, and the 2-minute-old update. A's offline state shows the data is stale through the design itself: the bus marker turns grey and is labeled 'Last known position', and the time reads 'Last known: about 6 minutes away'. It does this without repeating itself, and the Try again button is easy to reach with a thumb. B explains what happens next more clearly, but it says the 2-minute age three times, keeps the bus marker the same live yellow when offline, and fills the route with vague rows labeled 'Stop', which makes the screen feel busier than A's.

Both use the brief's facts correctly, and neither keeps the searched number in the empty state. B fits the volunteer's job better: each animal has a thumb-sized "Ear tag and health papers checked" checkbox, and its check-in button stays disabled until that box is ticked, which enforces the brief's verify-then-check-in rule. A only says "Check the ear tag and health papers first" in plain text. A's empty-state message is a little more useful because it covers the case where the number is right but no animals are entered yet, but B's serif type, weigh-in card and clear status pills make it look more like a finished product.

Both screens use the brief's facts correctly and make nothing up. B's check-in screen is clearer at a glance: 'Check in Biscuit' is a solid, obvious primary button, while A's greyed-out buttons look disabled and have weak contrast, even though A's tag-and-papers checkbox fits the workflow well. B's empty state is also more useful because it covers both a mistyped number and a correct number whose animals aren't entered yet. Neither empty screen keeps the number the volunteer searched for.

Both spell the name correctly, invent nothing, and set it in a similar default bold sans, so the decision comes down to the mark. A's blocky tree, with branch shapes cut out of a solid crown, is pixel-aligned and stays crisp and recognizable at 32 and 16 px, and its heavy shapes would survive embroidery and cut vinyl. B's mark turns blurry and anti-aliased at small sizes, has a thin trunk that doesn't connect to the canopy, and reads more like a lamp or airplane than a tree. Neither mark is very distinctive, but B is the weaker one.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing, and both use the same default bold sans in a plain lockup, so the marks decide it. B's chunky crown with a forked-branch cutout snaps to the pixel grid and stays crisp and solid at 16 and 32 px, which suits embroidery and vinyl. A's mark reads more like an umbrella or a lamp on a base than a tree, and its 16 px view goes soft and blurry. Neither idea gets far past a generic pixel tree, so B's lead is small.

Both spell the name exactly and invent nothing, and both hold up in one color and reversed. A's B is cut out of a gabled mill shape, which ties the mark to the 1940s feed mill. B is a plain heavy notched B that any company starting with B could use. B is sharper at 16 px, where A's inner letter blurs into grey, but A's building outline stays clear and its idea belongs to this client, which tips the choice.

Both spell the name correctly and add nothing invented. A's heavy B monogram, with its notched counters, keeps the same solid shape at 32 and 16 px and holds up in one ink and reversed, so it would stamp and embroider well. B tries to put a B inside a mill-like silhouette, but the B's bowls break out of the shape awkwardly, the thin white slivers turn to mush at 16 px, and at small sizes the mark looks more like a folder or printer icon than a feed mill. B has the more specific idea, but it fails the small-size and production test that matters more, and A is the cleaner, more deliberate piece of craft.

A runs off the bottom of the page: its logo panel and its fifth section ('Use it consistently') are cut off, and it gives Bank Plaster and Cream the same hex (#FFFDF7). B fits the whole system on one page, with a logo section, a role and use for every color, a fuller contrast table, a type scale shown at size, and say/not voice pairs drawn from real brief facts. B's only flaw is a small footer slip that lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg'; neither guide invents facts.

B runs off the bottom of the page: its logo block and the final 'use it consistently' section are cut off, so the logo display and usage rules are partly lost. Its color panel also leaves a large empty area. A fits the page and gives a fuller system: logo shown on three backgrounds with a clear-space rule, a named role for every color, a full contrast table and a type scale with sizes. Its voice and imagery do/don't lists are specific to this client and match B's. A's only flaws are minor: the footer lists 'logo.svg' twice and the audience line is a little odd.

Neither page invents facts. A states every color's job in plain words (page background, cards and forms, headlines and copy, logo and actions), names the services and the nervous-adult and toddler audiences, and its larger say/skip examples are easier to read and write from. B adds useful logo variants and shows its type scale at size, but its voice and imagery text is smaller, it leaves out the services, and it leaves a large empty band at the bottom of the page.

Neither guide invents any facts, and both use nearly the same teal palette, Source Serif 4 with Public Sans, and SAY/SKIP voice examples. B wins because it gives each color a plain-language role (page background, headlines and copy, captions and labels, logo and actions, text on teal), uses the brief's services and both audiences (nervous adults and toddlers), and fills the page evenly. A leaves a large empty band at the bottom and its color roles are vaguer. A does have one advantage: it shows the reversed logo on teal, which is useful for mailers.

A's offline screen is broken: a huge empty yellow panel fills the screen and pushes the bus card off the bottom, so the parent can't see the bus's last known position. A also makes up intermediate stops (Cedar St., Maple & 3rd). B shows the offline banner with the 2-minute timestamp and keeps the parent's place. B has its own faults: its route list is illogical, putting the bus after Maya's stop and listing 'Ridgeway Ave.' as a separate stop. It doesn't say the 6-minute estimate may be stale or what to do next, and its status bar is plain text instead of icons. Even so, B's states work and A's offline state does not.

nocouncil: Lakeview Elementary as a route stop
council: Lakeview School as a route stop
Ridgeway Ave. as a separate stop 2 stops away

verdicts.why: B's offline screen is broken: the offline banner grows to fill almost the whole screen and pushes the bus status off the bottom, so the parent can't see their child's bus at all. B also makes up stop names (Lakeview Elementary, Cedar St., Maple & 3rd) that aren't in the brief. A keeps the same screen when offline and adds a clear 'Last update 2 minutes ago' banner, but it has its own problems: its route line doesn't make sense (Bus 14 is listed as a stop after Maya's stop, and Ridgeway Ave. shows as 2 stops away), and its offline screen still shows '3 stops away / 6 min' without saying that this may be out of date.

council: 'Ridgeway Ave.' as a separate stop 2 stops away

verdicts.why: A's empty state keeps the place: it shows the number the volunteer searched, offers a fix (check the number or contact the 4-H office) and a clear way back. B clears the search field and only repeats the headline. A's per-animal action, 'Verify tag & health papers', matches the brief's check-in step, while B's plain 'Check in' drops that step. B also adds nav tabs (Exhibitors, Schedule) that the brief never mentions. A's one questionable addition is a 'Finish check-in' bar that sits oddly next to per-animal check-in.

council: bottom navigation with Exhibitors and Schedule tabs

verdicts.why: B builds the brief's real step into each action: every unchecked animal has a 'Verify tag & health papers' button and a clear status chip, while A uses a generic 'Check in' button. B's empty state shows the number that was searched, gives a real next step (check the number or contact the 4-H office) and leaves the number in the field. A's empty state clears the search field and repeats the headline, which loses the volunteer's place. B makes up a few extras, like a sample exhibitor number, a 'Finish check-in' footer and a 'contact the 4-H office' instruction, but A also adds a Schedule tab and a duplicate 'Breeding gilt' subtitle, and its states are thinner.

council: 'Exhibitors' search tab as a separate feature
